newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. election outcome sparks HK, Tokyo rallies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. election outcome sparks HK, Tokyo rallies.

text.p: Election fever swept Hong Kong and Tokyo stock markets on Wednesday as U.S. President Bill Clinton won a second term and the Republican party retained its control of Congress.
Although the reaction was more muted in most other Asian markets, a rally seized Hong Kong after an initially lukewarm response to Clinton's victory.
The win makes Clinton the first Democrat to be re-elected president in more than 50 years.
The Hang Seng Index reached an intra-day high of 12,799.11, before closing 272.77 points, or 2.18 percent, higher at a record 12,775.47.
Shares in Tokyo staged a similar run, leaving the key Nikkei 225 index up 399.19 points, or 1.94 percent, at 20,991.52.
"What is happening? One word -- election," said Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities in Hong Kong. "The result is filtering into the market as being the best of all worlds."

Traders view the combination of a Democrat president and Republican Congress as favourable for financial markets because it will keep both sides in check and avert any chance of a jolt to the U.S. economy from drastic fiscal policy changes.
"The Republicans keeping control of the House (of Representatives) eased fears of possible dollar falls and pushed up stocks," said Shigenori Okazaki, a political analyst at SBC Warburg.

He said a drop in the dollar could have sparked selling of U.S. stocks, which could have dragged down Tokyo stocks. But after the U.S. elections, the dollar rose above 114.40 yen in Tokyo afternoon trade.
Other Asian markets were more focused on local factors.

Taiwan's weighted index jumped 49.51 points, or 0.75 percent, to a year's high of 6,653.65 on continued buoyancy after the government's decision to allow a major state fund to invest in stocks and ease the investment cap on another.
Thai blue chips attracted buying by foreign investors who were bargain hunting after the market's recent sharp fall. The SET index closed up 24.26 points, or 2.64 percent, at 943.27.
Malaysia's composite index recouped earlier losses to close up 2.28 points, or 0.19 percent, at 1,179.09, while Singapore's Straits Times Index rose 10.22 points, or 0.49 percent, to 2,080.45.
Trade and consumer price index figures out on Wednesday helped bolster Indonesian shares, which gained 3.47 points, or 0.59 percent, to close at 587.34.

Seoul stocks rallied strongly on hopes the government would support the market, which fell to three-year lows on Monday and Tuesday. The composite index ended 13.64 points, or 1.86 percent, higher at 747.29.

In Pakistan, stocks jumped 5.25 percent on heavy buying triggered by the sacking of Prime Minister Benizar Bhutto's government on Tuesday, when markets were closed for a religous holiday. At close on Wednesday, Karachi's 100-share index was up 78.63 points at 1,577.40 after reaching an intra-day high of 1,607.84.
Manila's composite index edged up for the sixth straight session on selected bargain-hunting, gaining 11.25 points to 2,998.43 by the close.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index dipped 1.0 point 2,360.6 while New Zealand shares closed up 13.75 points at 2,325.21.
The dollar firmed in Tokyo, relieved at the U.S. election result and dealers said the Congressional results were particularly satisfying as their outcome had been less certain.
At 1142 GMT the U.S. unit was quoted at 113.95/114.05 yen and 1.5204/14 marks.
Hong Kong gold slid on overseas selling pressure, particularly from London, ending at US$378.10/60 against New York's $378.80/379.30 close on Tuesday.
SIMEX Brent December crude futures edged up eight cents from London's Tuesday settlement of $22.19 a barrel to $22.17.
